newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak VSZ sees diverisfying as key to future.
newsitem.headline: Slovak VSZ sees diverisfying as key to future.

text.p: VSZ a.s., Slovakia's largest steel maker, is looking to diversify in an attempt to shield itself from the cycles of the world steel market and boost its bottom line.

VSZ President Jan Smerek told Reuters that isolated metallurgical enterprises could no longer exist alone and new investments into enhanced steel production -- seen at 10 billion crowns ($320 million) -- would cost far more than VSZ could afford.

"We are aiming to diversify our capital to other business activities which we believe are more profitable than steelmaking and also partly to be prepared for a recession in the steel industry," he said.
Smerek said VSZ saw many opportunities in the fields of engineering, telecom, energy production and services both inside Slovakia and across central and eastern Europe.
"In Slovakia there are now opportunities for strong capitalised groups to diversify to other fields. So who else apart from us should do so?" Smerek said.
He said VSZ was still undecided on whether to invest in a new electrolytic zinc plating line for steel sheets.

VSZ has an offer already on the table from Czech car maker Skoda Auto a.s. to purchase the production from this new line, but the lure of ensured customers might fail to entice the firm since the low steel price expected from a former East Bloc mill left little room for profits.
Smerek said the diversification was being financed from external sources only, and that all of VSZ's new investments in fields other than metallurgy was "self-supporting and independent".
"We would devote only internal resources for the modernisation of our metallurgy production and we do not want to, nor are we, using this (external) money," he said.
He did not give any overall figure for the company's investments but said no new loans were needed at the moment.
"We have permanent credit offers and in addition our own loans are revolving and we have various forms of bonds," he said.
Smerek said that while the firm was in the enviable position of not needing to take on a strategic partner, it might seek out foreign partners for some of its ventures.

"We need foreign partners because we do not have the capacity to invest in something for which we have no know-how or the ability to take the risk, which would be big even for larger and better-known steelmills," he added.
"Perhaps other banks may lend us funds for capital participation in Bulgarian and Hungarian metallurgical enterprises where we have concrete plans," he said.
